items.atAGlance: Phở bò is Vietnam’s best-known noodle soup: clear, fragrant beef broth, soft rice noodles, and thin slices of beef finished with herbs. It feels light, comforting, and deeply satisfying.
items.goodToKnow: Herbs, lime, chili, and bean sprouts usually arrive on the side. Add them little by little so the broth stays balanced.

items.howToEnjoy: Taste the broth first, then add herbs, lime, bean sprouts, or chili a little at a time. Keep the seasoning balanced so the broth still leads.
items.worthKnowing: Phở is one of Vietnam’s signature noodle soups, with northern and southern styles differing in broth sweetness, herb plates, and condiments.

items.goodToKnow: Nước chấm is the usual sauce: fish sauce balanced with lime, sugar, garlic, and chili. Start with half, mix, then add more if the noodles need it.

items.howToEnjoy: Pour the nước chấm gradually, then mix so the beef juices, herbs, noodles, and crunch share the flavor. Ask for no chili or no peanuts before it is assembled.
items.worthKnowing: Nước chấm is the usual sauce: fish sauce balanced with lime, sugar, garlic, and chili. It is a dressing for the bowl, not a thick gravy.

items.atAGlance: Bún chả cá is rice vermicelli with springy fish cakes, herbs, fried shallots, and a light sauce or broth depending on the shop. It should taste seafood-savory, fresh, and gentle.
items.goodToKnow: Chả cá means fish cake here, not grilled pork. Ask whether it is served dry-style or with broth if the menu photo is unclear.

items.howToEnjoy: Taste the fish cakes first, then add herbs, chili, or sauce gradually. If it comes with broth, sip before adding lime or chili.
items.worthKnowing: Chả cá means fish cake in this dish. It is separate from Bún chả, the grilled-pork vermicelli dish, even though the names look close.

items.englishTranslation: Vermicelli with tofu and shrimp paste
items.atAGlance: Bún đậu mắm tôm is a northern-style platter of rice vermicelli, fried tofu, herbs, and pungent shrimp-paste sauce. It is salty, vivid, and defined by the sauce.
items.goodToKnow: Mắm tôm is fermented shrimp-paste sauce with a strong aroma. Many places can offer a milder nước chấm dip if you ask.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một phần bún đậu mắm tôm.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one order of vermicelli with tofu and shrimp paste.

items.whatItIs: Bún đậu mắm tôm is a platter of rice vermicelli, fried tofu, herbs, and pungent shrimp-paste sauce, often with pork or other add-ons. It is vivid, salty, and very different from a tidy noodle bowl.
items.howToEnjoy: Try the sauce carefully first; mắm tôm is strong even for confident eaters. If the aroma feels like too much, ask whether a milder fish-sauce dip is available.
items.worthKnowing: Bún đậu mắm tôm is closely tied to casual northern-style snacking and sharing. The sauce is the point, so it is worth knowing before you order.
items.travelerCaution: Contains shrimp paste and may include pork.

items.englishTranslation: Duck and bamboo shoot vermicelli soup
items.atAGlance: Bún măng vịt is duck and bamboo shoot vermicelli soup. The broth is savory and warming, while herbs and ginger dipping sauce keep the duck from feeling heavy.
items.goodToKnow: Duck often comes with a ginger fish-sauce dip on the side. Use it for the meat, then taste the broth before adding extra chili.

items.whatItIs: Bún măng vịt is duck and bamboo shoot vermicelli soup. The broth is savory and warming, with bamboo shoots adding earthy crunch and herbs brightening the duck.
items.howToEnjoy: Taste the broth first, then use the ginger fish-sauce dip for the duck. Add herbs and chili gradually so the bamboo shoot flavor still comes through.
items.worthKnowing: Duck noodle soups often depend on the side dip as much as the broth. Ginger, fish sauce, and chili cut through the richness of the duck.

items.atAGlance: Cao lầu is a Hội An noodle bowl with chewy noodles, pork, herbs, crisp bits, and a small amount of seasoned pork sauce. It is more concentrated and local-specialty than soup-like.
items.goodToKnow: The sauce lightly coats the noodles instead of flooding the bowl. Mix well so the pork, herbs, and crisp topping share the seasoning.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một phần cao lầu.

items.whatItIs: Cao lầu is a Hội An noodle bowl with chewy noodles, pork, herbs, crisp bits, and just enough sauce to coat everything. It feels more like a composed local specialty than a soup.
items.howToEnjoy: Mix the bowl so the sauce reaches the noodles, herbs, and pork. Add chili slowly if you want heat without losing the chewy noodle flavor.
items.worthKnowing: Cao lầu is strongly associated with Hội An. The noodles, herbs, pork, and restrained sauce are part of the dish’s local identity.
items.travelerCaution: May contain pork.

items.atAGlance: Mì Quảng gà is a central-Vietnam noodle dish with wide turmeric rice noodles, chicken, herbs, peanuts, rice crackers, and just enough broth to coat the bowl.
items.goodToKnow: Mì Quảng is not a normal soup. The turmeric broth is shallow and concentrated, so mix before judging whether it needs lime or chili.

items.englishTranslation: Broken rice with grilled pork chop
items.atAGlance: Cơm tấm sườn is a classic broken-rice plate with a grilled pork chop, pickles, scallion oil, and dipping sauce. It is smoky, savory, and easy to order for lunch or dinner.
items.goodToKnow: A fried egg is a common upgrade. Pour the sauce slowly so the rice gets flavor without becoming too wet.

items.worthKnowing: Cơm tấm is especially associated with southern Vietnam and Saigon-style everyday eating, where broken rice became a beloved base for grilled pork plates.
items.travelerCaution: May contain pork.

items.howToEnjoy: Add sauce slowly and taste as you go. A fried egg, extra rice, or pickles can make the plate easier to share or finish.
items.worthKnowing: Cơm tấm bì chả sườn is associated with southern Vietnam. That link tells you where the dish’s local identity is strongest, even though recipes still shift by city, shop, and family style.

items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht fuhn baw kaw banh mee
items.whatItIs: Bánh mì bò kho is Vietnamese beef stew served with bread for dipping. The bowl brings tender beef, carrots, warm spice, herbs, and broth that the baguette is meant to catch.
items.howToEnjoy: Tear the bread and dip it into the stew while the broth is hot. Add herbs, lime, or chili gradually so the warm spice stays balanced.
items.worthKnowing: This order shows another side of bánh mì: bread as a tool for broth, not just a sandwich. Bò kho itself is a Vietnamese comfort stew with beef, carrots, and aromatics.

items.atAGlance: Bánh mì pate is a Vietnamese bread order with pâté sandwich, pickles, herbs, and a crisp baguette or soft bun. It is quick, satisfying, and easy to eat on the go.
items.goodToKnow: If the bread is not already toasted, you can ask for it toasted for more crunch.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ổ bánh mì pate.

items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht oh bahn mee pah-tay
items.whatItIs: Bánh mì pate is a bánh mì sandwich with pâté, pickled vegetables, herbs, and usually sauce or pâté depending on the shop. The crisp bread and sharp pickles keep the filling lively.
items.howToEnjoy: Ask for no chili if you are heat-sensitive. Bread orders are best soon after they are made, while the texture is still fresh.
items.worthKnowing: Vietnamese bread orders are shaped by local fillings, herbs, pickles, sauces, and quick street-service habits, not just the bread itself.
items.travelerCaution: May contain pork.

items.worthKnowing: These rolls are often called fresh spring rolls in English, which helps distinguish them from fried chả giò or nem rán.

items.worthKnowing: Street snacks vary by region and stall, so the same name may look a little different from place to place. The sauce and texture are often the best clues.

items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay soo-uh dah
items.whatItIs: Cà phê sữa đá is strong Vietnamese robusta coffee mixed with sweetened condensed milk and poured over ice. It is bold, creamy, and made for hot afternoons.
items.howToEnjoy: Stir well before drinking so the condensed milk lifts through the coffee. Ask for less sweet or more ice if you want it lighter.
items.worthKnowing: This is the everyday icon of Vietnamese iced coffee. The flavor comes from robusta strength, condensed milk sweetness, and a slow phin drip.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê đen đá is strong phin-brewed black coffee poured over ice. It is bold, bitter, and refreshing when you want the Vietnamese coffee hit without condensed milk.
items.goodToKnow: This is the unsweetened or lightly sweetened black-coffee lane. Ask for đường riêng if you want sugar on the side.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê đen đá.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of Vietnamese iced black coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay den dah
items.whatItIs: Cà phê đen đá is iced black Vietnamese coffee. Without condensed milk, the robusta comes through darker, sharper, and more refreshing over ice.
items.howToEnjoy: Sip before adding sugar. If it is stronger than expected, ask for more ice or sugar on the side instead of turning it into milk coffee.
items.worthKnowing: This is the cleanest way to taste the coffee base behind many Vietnamese café drinks: phin-brewed, bold, and often more intense than a typical American iced coffee.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê sữa nóng is hot Vietnamese milk coffee: phin-brewed robusta softened with condensed milk. It is sweet, strong, and better when you want the café ritual without ice.
items.goodToKnow: The condensed milk settles low in the cup. Stir until the color evens out, then decide whether you want it stronger next time.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê sữa nóng.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of hot Vietnamese milk coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay soo-uh nawng
items.whatItIs: Cà phê sữa nóng is hot phin coffee with condensed milk. It keeps the sweet, creamy Vietnamese coffee profile but drops the ice.
items.howToEnjoy: Stir from the bottom so the condensed milk fully blends into the coffee. Drink it slowly while the cup is still warm.
items.worthKnowing: Hot milk coffee is useful in rainy weather, air-conditioned cafés, or early mornings when iced coffee feels too sharp.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê đen nóng is hot black Vietnamese coffee from a phin filter. It is sharper, more aromatic, and more intense than the milk versions.
items.goodToKnow: Order this when you want the robusta flavor to lead. Ask for sugar on the side if you do not want it pre-sweetened.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê đen nóng.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of hot black coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay den nawng
items.whatItIs: Cà phê đen nóng is hot black Vietnamese coffee, usually phin-brewed and served small, strong, and aromatic.
items.howToEnjoy: Treat it like a slow strong cup, not a large mug. Ask for sugar separately if you want to control the sweetness.
items.worthKnowing: This order is a good bridge between espresso habits and Vietnamese phin culture: concentrated like a short coffee, but brewed with a different rhythm.

items.atAGlance: Bạc xỉu is a softer, milkier coffee with more sweet milk than coffee. It is creamy, gentle, and a good pick if regular Vietnamese coffee feels too strong.
items.goodToKnow: Think of it as coffee-flavored milk rather than a heavy caffeine hit. It is often served iced.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly bạc xỉu.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of light milk coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee bak see-ew
items.whatItIs: Bạc xỉu is a milkier, gentler coffee drink with more sweet milk than coffee. It is creamy and friendly if regular Vietnamese coffee feels too strong.
items.howToEnjoy: Order it iced when you want something cool and soft. Think of it as coffee-flavored milk rather than a heavy caffeine hit.
items.worthKnowing: Bạc xỉu is closely associated with Saigon and Chợ Lớn café culture. The idea is simple and charming: lots of milk, just enough coffee.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê trứng is Hanoi’s famous egg coffee: strong coffee under a whipped egg-yolk cream that drinks like warm tiramisu. It is rich, sweet, and worth trying slowly.
items.goodToKnow: The egg is whipped into a custardy foam, not cooked like breakfast eggs. Ask whether it is served hot or iced before ordering.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê trứng.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of egg coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay choong
items.whatItIs: Cà phê trứng is Hanoi-born egg coffee: strong coffee topped with whipped egg-yolk cream, sugar, and condensed milk. It tastes more like a warm coffee custard than a normal cup.
items.howToEnjoy: Try the foam first, then stir if you want the creamy layer to blend into the coffee. Order it when you want a small dessert-like café moment.
items.worthKnowing: Egg coffee is one of Vietnam’s most famous coffee creations and is strongly tied to Hanoi café culture. The backstory often points to resourceful cafés making richness from scarce milk.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê cốt dừa is coconut coffee, often served cold with creamy coconut blended or layered against strong coffee. It feels tropical, rich, and almost dessert-like.
items.goodToKnow: This can be closer to a café treat than a plain coffee. Ask for less sweet if you want the coffee bitterness to stay visible.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê cốt dừa.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of coconut coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay koht yoo-uh
items.whatItIs: Cà phê cốt dừa is coconut coffee, usually cold, creamy, and layered or blended so coconut sweetness meets strong Vietnamese coffee.
items.howToEnjoy: Let it soften for a moment if it arrives icy or blended. Stir lightly when you want the coconut and coffee to mix instead of staying in layers.
items.worthKnowing: Coconut coffee shows the modern playful side of Vietnamese cafés: still built on a bold coffee base, but closer to a tropical dessert drink.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê muối is salt coffee, a creamy Vietnamese coffee with a lightly salted foam that makes the bitter robusta taste rounder and more caramel-like.
items.goodToKnow: The salt should balance the sweetness, not taste like seawater. It is strongly associated with Huế-style café creativity.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê muối.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of salt coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay moo-ee
items.whatItIs: Cà phê muối is salt coffee: robusta coffee with sweet milk and a lightly salted cream. The salt makes the cup taste round, rich, and caramel-like.
items.howToEnjoy: Sip before judging the salt. A good cup should feel balanced, with the salt sharpening the cream and softening the coffee bitterness.
items.worthKnowing: Salt coffee is especially associated with Huế, and it has spread because the sweet-salty balance feels both familiar and surprising.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê phin is Vietnamese drip coffee brewed through the small metal filter sitting on the cup. Order it when you want the slow, classic coffee ritual itself.
items.goodToKnow: Phin coffee takes a few minutes. The pause is normal: the drip, the glass, and the slow first sip are part of Vietnamese café culture.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê phin.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of Vietnamese drip coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay fin
items.whatItIs: Cà phê phin is coffee brewed through Vietnam’s small metal drip filter. It is less a flavor name than a way of making and waiting for the cup.
items.howToEnjoy: Give the drip time. When the filter finishes, stir if milk is present, add ice if you want it cold, and taste before changing sweetness.
items.worthKnowing: The phin filter is part of the social rhythm of Vietnamese cafés: order, sit, watch the drip, then linger over a strong small glass.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê sữa tươi is coffee with fresh milk instead of only condensed milk. It is still Vietnamese coffee, but smoother, lighter, and less sticky-sweet.
items.goodToKnow: This is a useful middle lane if condensed milk feels too heavy but black coffee feels too sharp.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê sữa tươi.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of coffee with fresh milk.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay soo-uh too-ee
items.whatItIs: Cà phê sữa tươi is Vietnamese coffee with fresh milk. Compared with condensed-milk coffee, it usually tastes lighter, smoother, and less syrupy.
items.howToEnjoy: Choose it when you want milk coffee without the full sweetness of condensed milk. Ask for less sugar if the café sweetens it separately.
items.worthKnowing: Fresh-milk coffee is common in modern cafés, where Vietnamese coffee habits meet latte-style preferences.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê đá xay is blended iced coffee, a cold café drink where coffee, ice, milk, or cream become a thick shake-like cup.
items.goodToKnow: Expect a dessert texture more than a sidewalk phin coffee. Ask for less sugar if you want it less sweet.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê đá xay.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of blended iced coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay dah sai
items.whatItIs: Cà phê đá xay is blended iced coffee, usually coffee, ice, milk or cream, and sugar turned into a thick café drink.
items.howToEnjoy: Treat it like a cold dessert coffee. Ask for less sugar or more coffee if you want the drink less sweet and more grown-up.
items.worthKnowing: This is the menu item for modern air-conditioned cafés, not the sidewalk phin ritual. It is still useful when you want a cold familiar order.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê latte is the familiar milk-forward latte found in modern Vietnamese cafés. It is useful when you want a softer coffee order in an international café setting.
items.goodToKnow: This is not the classic phin drink, but many city cafés offer it beside Vietnamese coffee styles.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê latte.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of latte.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay lah-tay
items.whatItIs: Cà phê latte is a latte-style coffee order with milk. It is the safer familiar choice in cafés that also serve espresso drinks.
items.howToEnjoy: Ask whether it is hot or iced if the menu does not say. If you want a Vietnamese-style cup, choose phin coffee instead.
items.worthKnowing: Vietnam’s café scene now includes both traditional phin drinks and global espresso drinks, so latte can be useful even though it is not the local classic.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê espresso is a short, concentrated coffee order in modern cafés. It is quick, strong, and different from the slower phin style.
items.goodToKnow: Use this word in espresso-machine cafés. At traditional coffee shops, a black phin coffee may be the more natural strong order.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê espresso.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of espresso.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay ess-press-oh
items.whatItIs: Cà phê espresso is espresso, a short concentrated coffee from an espresso machine rather than a phin filter.
items.howToEnjoy: Use this in modern cafés where espresso machines are visible. In a traditional shop, ask for black phin coffee instead.
items.worthKnowing: Espresso belongs to Vietnam’s modern café layer, but it is not the same experience as watching coffee drip through a phin.

items.atAGlance: Cà phê mocha is coffee with chocolate and milk, a modern café drink for when you want coffee but also something sweet and dessert-like.
items.goodToKnow: It is familiar and easy in bigger cafés, but it will not tell you as much about Vietnam’s phin coffee culture as the local styles do.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly cà phê mocha.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of mocha coffee.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee kah fay moh-kah
items.whatItIs: Cà phê mocha is coffee with milk and chocolate. It is sweet, soft, and familiar when you want dessert energy more than a classic Vietnamese coffee.
items.howToEnjoy: Ask for less sweet if you want the coffee to show through. It can be hot or iced depending on the café.
items.worthKnowing: Mocha belongs to Vietnam’s modern café menu layer. The cultural story is stronger in phin, egg, salt, coconut, and bạc xỉu drinks.

items.atAGlance: Trà đá is plain iced tea, often served automatically at casual restaurants and street-food spots. It is light, unsweetened or barely sweet, and good with rich food.
items.goodToKnow: It may come free or very cheap, depending on the place. Bottled tea is a different order.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly trà đá.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of iced tea.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee chah dah
items.whatItIs: Trà đá is an iced tea. Depending on the style, it can be plain and light or sweet enough to feel like a dessert drink.
items.howToEnjoy: Ask for less sweet before it is mixed. Plain tea is light with meals; milk tea and fruit tea can be dessert-like.
items.worthKnowing: Tea ranges from plain meal tea to sweet fruit or milk tea. The same English word can cover very different drinks.

items.atAGlance: Trà nóng is a simple hot tea order, usually served in a cup or small pot. It is light, calming, and good beside a meal.
items.goodToKnow: Iced tea may come very cold and light. Hot tea is usually served in a cup or small pot.

items.atAGlance: Sinh tố bơ is a thick smoothie made with avocado, usually blended with ice and milk or condensed milk. It is cool, creamy, and fruit-forward.
items.goodToKnow: If you do not want dairy, ask before ordering; many stalls add milk by default.
items.quickSayVietnamese: Cho tôi một ly sinh tố bơ.
items.quickSayEnglish: I’d like one glass of avocado smoothie.
items.quickSaySoundOut: chaw toy moht lee sing toh buh
items.whatItIs: Sinh tố bơ is a smoothie with avocado, ice, and often milk or condensed milk. It is cool, creamy, and closer to dessert than plain juice.
items.howToEnjoy: Ask for less sugar or no condensed milk if you want more fruit flavor. Many smoothies are thick enough to feel like dessert.
items.worthKnowing: Smoothies are a warm-weather café and street-stall comfort. Condensed milk can make them richer and sweeter than a typical US smoothie.

items.atAGlance: Sinh tố xoài is a thick mango smoothie, usually blended with ice and milk or condensed milk. It is bright, creamy, and dessert-like.
items.goodToKnow: Ask for less sugar or less condensed milk if you want the fruit flavor to lead.

items.howToEnjoy: Ask for less sugar or no condensed milk if you want more fruit flavor. Many smoothies are thick enough to feel like dessert.
items.worthKnowing: Smoothies are a warm-weather café and street-stall comfort. Condensed milk can make them richer and sweeter than a typical US smoothie.

items.atAGlance: Sinh tố dâu is a thick smoothie made with strawberry, usually blended with ice and milk or condensed milk. It is cool, creamy, and fruit-forward.
